name: Chloe Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the business reporter on the website of the Harbour Gazette, the daily paper for our port town and the villages around it. My patch is local firms, the port, shop openings and closures, and the industrial estate. Most mornings I'm reading company filings and press releases, then I ring people, and I try to get out to one business a week in person. I like the shop owners who tell you everything; I'm tired of being asked to write five quick posts a day for the website.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They merged the business and news desks in the summer, so there are fewer of us and more targets. My editor Paul is fair but stretched. I'm on a lower wage than the reporters who joined before the merger.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ravi, who's in the second year of an electrician apprenticeship, in a rented flat by the marina, though not the nice end. Between us we've got under a month's money saved. I use AI now and then to summarise company accounts, but I always check the numbers myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for summarising annual reports and not much else, which is about right. At work I'd say let's stop chasing the next shiny thing and fix the website targets. Online I'd stay neutral, as I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the merger already did what people think AI would do. We lost three people and nobody replaced them. AI turning out to be hype doesn't undo a merger that took three people off the Harbour Gazette newsroom in one afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summary tool for filings, because it saves me an hour a week. I'd look at jobs in press offices around the port, quietly, because they pay better. And I'd keep trying to put fifty a month away, though some months that fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, the same as I already feel. Not dramatic, just tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would be the first to slip if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance, probably, because it's annual and we could switch. Then my phone contract. We'd never be late on the rent, because the landlord's already looking for reasons to put it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually leave for a press office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the money was right and it was a real company, yes. The port authority's comms team pays maybe a fifth more. I'd miss reporting, but I'd also be able to save.

say: I'd say AI is useful for **annual reports** and not much else.
I'd tell colleagues to fix the **website targets** instead of chasing shiny things.
think: The **merger** already did what people expect AI to do.
We lost **three people** and none were replaced.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** for company filings.
Quietly look at **press office** jobs around the port.
Try to save **fifty a month**, even though some months fail.
feel: **Tense and tired**, the same as she already feels.
S0.quote: AI turning out to be hype doesn't undo a merger that took three people off the Harbour Gazette newsroom in one afternoon.
fieldNote: The **desk merger** is her real shock, and AI hype changes nothing.
A **port comms job** paying a fifth more is a live option.
She'd protect the **rent** above everything, fearing the landlord.

steps.text: Keep using the AI summary tool for company accounts
Apply to the port authority's communications team
Set a fifty-pound monthly transfer into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every business desk is going to be smaller, and we need to show readers what humans add. At work I'd ask Paul which tasks we hand over first. Online I'd stay measured, maybe share a sensible article.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, half my day is turning press releases and company accounts into short posts, and that's exactly what goes. What's left is visiting firms and building contacts, which I'm not great at yet. If software writes the shop-opening posts, the Harbour Gazette needs one business reporter, and that person probably isn't the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly now, since other reporters have shown they work, and use the saved hours to get out to the industrial estate twice a week. I'd apply to the port authority comms team within the year as a backup. And I'd start doing a short evening course in business finance, to get better at reading accounts myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like a race I'm not sure I'm fast enough for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the newsroom would you be most worried for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who does the court lists and the announcements. She's sixty and brilliant on the phone, but her work is all the routine stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ravi think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi thinks he's fine because he's on tools, and he's probably right for a while. He says I should come into the trade with him, which makes me laugh, but I don't completely rule it out.

say: I'd say business desks will shrink and we must show **what humans add**.
I'd ask Paul which **tasks go first**, and stay measured online.
think: Half my day is turning **press releases** into posts, which goes first.
The newsroom might keep one business reporter, likely **not the junior**.
do: Learn the tools now and spend saved hours on **site visits**.
Apply to the **port comms team** within the year as a backup.
Take an evening course in **business finance**.
feel: **Anxious**, like a race she isn't sure she can **win**.
S1.quote: If software writes the shop-opening posts, the Harbour Gazette needs one business reporter, and that person probably isn't the junior.
fieldNote: She uses the tools only once **others have proven** them, as here.
Her weakest skill, **building contacts**, is the one that survives.
Ravi's **trade job** gives the household a steadier earner for now.

steps.text: Use AI for filings and visit the industrial estate twice a week
Apply to the port authority comms team within a year
Take an evening course in reading business accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs serious government planning, and I'd say it calmly, because panicking doesn't help. At work I'd ask for honest answers about the newsroom. I'd probably write a piece on what local firms are doing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be gone within the first year after 2028, and so would the comms jobs I was eyeing. That's what scares me most, the backup goes at the same time. My back-up plan was a port press office, and a press office is thinking work too, so the plan and the job go together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny I could for the next two years, maybe cancel the gym and the streaming. I'd look seriously at joining Ravi in the electrical trade, because the card says hands-on robots come three years later. I'd talk to his boss about taking on a mate's labourer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not hysterical, but I'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap for robots change things at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi's wage becomes the one that lasts. He'd be qualified by then, so he's looking at maybe 2031 before robots catch up with electricians. That buys us time, but only if I'm earning something too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I might have to change careers at twenty-nine, and that it's not because I failed. My mum would worry I wasted my degree.

say: I'd say calmly that this needs **government planning**.
I'd ask for **honest answers** about the newsroom's future.
I'd write a piece on what **local firms** are doing about it.
think: I'd be gone within **a year** after 2028.
My **backup plan** in comms disappears at the same time.
do: Cancel the **gym and streaming** and save everything for two years.
Ask Ravi's boss about work as an **electrician's labourer**.
S2.quote: My back-up plan was a port press office, and a press office is thinking work too, so the plan and the job go together.
fieldNote: She spots that her **comms backup** is thinking work too.
The **robot delay** makes Ravi's trade the household's lifeline.
Her **centre** outlook shows in calm, practical language even when scared.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and streaming to save for two years
Ask Ravi's boss about a labourer job on his electrical team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable if people start now. I'd want the paper to be honest about its plans. Online I'd share practical guides, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three good years in journalism and then it'd shrink to nothing. I'd be thirty-two, which is fine to change, but we'd have very little saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools well, so I last as long as possible. By year two I'd start an evening electrical course, because Ravi would be qualified and could help me. And I'd try to get the savings up to three months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with a plan. Five years means I'd be studying wiring diagrams at night while still writing about the port in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is training as an electrician a real plan or a joke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It started as a joke. Then I looked at what's left after 2031 that isn't hands-on, and it's not much for someone like me. So it's real, if scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the business beat? Anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop owners. Mr Demir (who runs the bakery on the quay) tells me everything happening on the high street. I'd miss that kind of chat.

say: I'd say five years is **short but workable** if people start now.
I'd share **practical guides** online, not doom.
think: I'd get about **three good years** in journalism before it shrinks.
Changing at **thirty-two** is fine, but we'd have little saved.
do: Learn the tools well to **last longer** in the newsroom.
Start an evening **electrical course** by year two.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd be studying wiring diagrams at night while still writing about the port in the day.
fieldNote: The **electrician** idea moves from joke to real plan here.
She expects to **lose reporting** by around 2031 regardless.
She'd miss **shopkeepers** like Mr Demir more than the work itself.

steps.text: Use the newsroom AI tools daily to stay useful longer
Start an evening electrical installation course in year two
Build savings to three months of bills by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone time to plan, so there's no excuse for chaos. I'd say businesses and government should share the costs of retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is fine for me, honestly, if I use it. I can stay a business reporter for six or seven years, get better, save more. I'd plan to switch at around thirty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools as they're proven and become a better reporter, especially at visiting firms. I'd keep the electrical course as a slow plan, starting maybe year five. And Ravi and I would think about buying somewhere small, which we can't now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but it's a normal kind of worry. With ten years I get to finish becoming a reporter before I have to stop being one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the last couple of years before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd want the trade qualification done, and maybe be working part-time in both. The paper might still want someone to visit firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything still keeping you up at night in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, always. Ten years of lower pay doesn't build much. But it's better than two.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for chaos.
I'd want **businesses and government** to share retraining costs.
think: Ten years is **fine for me** if I use it.
I'd plan to **switch** careers at around thirty-four.
do: Learn tools as they're proven and get better at **visiting firms**.
Start the **electrical course** slowly around year five.
Look at **buying a small place** with Ravi.
feel: **Anxious** in a **normal** way, mostly about money.
S4.quote: With ten years I get to finish becoming a reporter before I have to stop being one.
fieldNote: Time lets her **grow as a reporter** first, then switch.
Buying a home becomes thinkable, a sign of **lower pressure**.
**Low pay** keeps her worried even with a decade.

steps.text: Visit two local firms a week to build business contacts
Begin an electrical installation course around year five
Save toward a deposit on a small flat with Ravi

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My plan and my backup both vanish, and we wouldn't have the money to ride it out. What would help is paid retraining for people moving into trades, so I could earn while learning, like Ravi does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what readers lose. When a shop on the quay closes, a machine can tell you it shut, but only a person can find out the rent tripled.

headlineQuote: When a shop on the quay closes, a machine can tell you it shut, but only a person can find out the rent tripled.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** business reporter at a port town's daily paper, after a **desk merger**.
She lives with Ravi, an **apprentice electrician**, and they have under a month saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once others have proven them.
She notices early that her **comms backup** is thinking work too, so it fails in AGI scenarios.
Over time her plan shifts toward **the electrical trade**, using the robot delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and her backup plan **vanish**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so she could earn while moving into a **trade**.
